Nelson Mandela Bay Water

By: Stenette Grosskopf | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Nelson Mandela Bay is the said to run out of water within the next 2-3 weeks!

Unique Selling Point:
It is projected that Nelson Mandela Bay (PE) will face Day Zero before the end of June! Almost 1.5 million residents will find themselves with dry taps within a matter of weeks. The dams supplying the urban areas only have about 12.3% of usable water left.

Yes, we have been here before — an in the case of CT — but at least Cape Town was prepared. It seems that the bulk of Gqeberha residents are either blissfully unaware or have a head-in-the-sand approach to this looming crisis. NMBM Residents are currently using around 299ML of water per day, while demand should have been limited to around 230ML, according to experts. And the seasonal rain forecast until September doesn’t offer much hope.

Summary:
Persistent drought has plagued the NMBM for over a decade. In 2010 the Metro was on the verge of a Day Zero event. Plans were made, systems suggested and residents came to the party... The threat was averted. From 2011 to 2016, the catchment areas received moderate rain and everyone forgot about the once looming crisis. But climate change has affected the region's rainfall and dam levels have been dropping. They have now reached a point of no return. With little rain forecast for the next few months, the combined usable dam levels sits at about 12% for the Metro. Taps are running dry. The city is needing to divert water earmarked for sanitation to desperate water users. Infrastructure is crumbling and continuous blackouts are not helping.

It seems no lessons were learnt from 2010.

Further information:
The Nelson Mandela Bay Metro replies on 4x water systems. The Kromme System supplies the main city of PE and it is estimated that the Impofu and Churchill dams have about 20 and 27 days of usable water left, respectively. The Kouga system comprises the Kouga and the Loerie dam. This system is 42% full, but not all the water is earmarked for NMB. A lot is used up by the Gamtoos Irrigation Board for farmers irrigating their crops. Then there is the much smaller Groendal dam which services Uitenhage.

Recognising that NMBM would need additional water in the future, the Nooitgedacht Water Transfer Scheme was commissioned in 1993. The project that would transfer 70ML of water from the Gariep dam to the Nooitgedacht Water Treatment Works outside PE was eventually started in 2010. Destined to be completed in 2014 - at a cost of R850million - the first drops from the scheme reached the city of Gqeberha (formerly PE) in March 2022. Just in time... but this is by no means a magic bullet. The system was designed to deliver 70ML per day, and can currently deliver 190ML per day at full capacity. But there is no contingency for when the system goes down. If there is loadshedding people will simply not have water. AND.. there will not be enough for everyone.

Extra Budget Items:
Fuel - Driving from Johannesburg to PE and back.
Accommodation: 1x night at Gariep for 3 people -- 1x night PE for 3x people -- additional 2x nights for 2x people
Flight for Presenter from PE to Jhb

Script:


NELSON MANDELA BAY WATER – MASTER


V/O
Parts of the Eastern Cape gripped by severe drought…dams supplying Nelson Mandela Metro fast running empty… residents urged to drastically cut consumption…the region declared an official disaster area as national government steps in.

The year: 2010!
LINK
Long before Cape Town’s Day Zero scare, the city that was formerly known as PE – now Gqeberha – was facing dry taps. Through a series of interventions they managed to avert disaster… Recognising that climate change is having a marked impact on the region’s rainfall, plans were drafted to future-proof the water supply for the region…
V/o
Fast forward to 2022… while some of the country has been enjoying generous seasonal summer rains, the southern Eastern Cape region remains dry, the warning signs of the past 12 years apparently largely ignored…
SUNRISE

Saturday 11 June 2022 06H30 am




V/O
As the sun hovers just below the horizon, the city of Gqeberha awakens. …
V/O
But underneath this calm, idyllic exterior there is a crisis in the making. The Bay’s water storage dams are at less than 12 percent capacity.. and for the 1.5 million local residents, the threat of a real Day Zero scenario is right on their doorstep…
Many suburbs and townships are already experiencing persistent water outages… forcing people to either buy water or collect it from water points…




Mimi Snoek
Masa: How long have you not had water?
Mimi: I think it’s after Easter. April, May, June… It’s June now.
V/O
Mimi Snoek lives in KwaNobuhle on the outskirts of the city. Every day she sets out with her bucket to look for water.
Mimi Snoek
Masa: This is quite heavy without the water.
Mimi: If I’m tired I stand next to the pavement, take a break. Walk, take a break.
V/O
She patiently waits her turn at the jojo tank. Fetching water is generally a chore for the children… but Mimi lives alone. And she can only use what she can carry…
Mimi Snoek
The floors, washing.. And wash myself. Everything.
V/O
Through hardship she has learnt the value of water.


Must put the dirty water, the washing water in another basin for use in the toilet. It's important, very important, the toilet Ma’am…. It’s difficult. No rain… We must pray for the rain…
Guy Rogers
Our dams have been steadily dwindling ever since 2015, probably. That was our last good rain. So, we’ve kind of had seven years of drought…
V/O
Guy Rogers – local resident and senior journalist at the Herald and Weekend Post – has been reporting on the region’s water woes for well over a decade.
Guy Rogers
There was quite a concerted effort by the previous council that was running things in the Bay to identify problem areas. But, you know, then the council changed, the leadership changed, and then and then there's a bit of rain. And so they take their eye off the ball.
Siyabulela Mama
In 2018 We were also on the verge of Day Zero and the ailing infrastructure in our water system was never fixed.
V/O
Siyabulela Mama, activist and member of the Nelson Mandela Bay Water Crisis Committee, is critical of the current Metro administration – a cobbled-together multi-party coalition led by the ANC
Siyabulela Mama
The situation is still here. We still have a coalition government that also faces the same political crisis where people are discussing who should be a city manager, who should not be a city manager … who should lead the coalition and who should not lead the coalition and there’s no serious debate and serious solutions around the water crisis.
V/O
The Water Crisis Committee is looking to be a part of the solution for the region’s ongoing water problems by giving a voice to the local communities.
Siyabulela Mama
We hear what business is saying, we hear what the government, the state is saying… but we don’t hear what communities are saying.
V/O
And you only need to spend a few hours talking to the people in the townships to realize they feel unheard.
Siyabonga Matika
When it comes to the time of voting, they do come to the people, but when it comes to the problems people are facing they don’t see them. I’m saying to you for the first 4 or 5 months in my area, Ward 46 and Ward 47 not a single councillor called a meeting.
V/O
The Metro’s water supply comes from a series of dams in the region – with the Churchill and Impofu dams on the Kromme River supplying the bulk of the Bay’s water. But these dams are so empty that the Municipality is literally slurping up the last drops of muddy water to meet the demand… which is currently about 280ML per day..
Siyabulela Mama
The municipality is planning to drill boreholes in August… This is in August, while we’re on the verge of this crisis now…
V/O
But besides the planned drilling, there is a glimmer of hope for the Nelson Mandela Bay Metro… and it comes all the way from the Free State / Eastern Cape border…
LINK
This is the Gariep dam – second largest dam in South Africa – It supplies water to parts of the Vaal, the city of Bloemfontein … but also, it’s a very important source for Nelson Mandela Bay.
V/O
In the 70’s an 82km irrigation tunnel was built from the dam, all the way to the great Fish River, to supply the central Eastern Cape with additional water… In the 1990’s the system was extended…
LINK
From the Southern tip of the Gariep dam millions of liters of water get transferred on a daily basis as far as Nelson Mandela Bay. Question is… is it enough?
V/O
From this intake tower – some 20kms upstream from the dam wall – the water travels through the irrigation tunnel… And from the Great Fish River, it is transferred via a series of channels, tunnels and rivers… all the way to the Nooitgedacht Water Treatment Works, about an hour’s drive outside Gqeberha.
V/O
We are met by acting Chief Executive for Amatola Water, Siyabulela Koyo…
Siyabulela Koyo
UPSOUND>>> This is where we are, coming all the way from Gariep – …
V/O
The first phase of the Nooitgedacht Water Transfer Scheme brought 70Mega Litres of water per day to the Metro. By 2018 the amount of water doubled… And as of the end of March this year … 210Mega L of water is now transferred to the bay on a daily basis.
Siyabulela Koyo
Masa: So with phase 3, how long did that take for you to increase that capacity?

Siya: The project started in 2017. It was supposed to run for about 44 months but there was a number of challenges during the implementation.

Masa: yes, there were many delays, hey?

Siya: Ja there were many delays. Funding issues, availability of funds to continue with the project.
V/O
But getting all this water to the plant is only part of the challenge… At the moment it only services the eastern parts of the Metro… So, over 100 suburbs on the western side of the Bay - that solely rely on the dams - are left dry…
Guy Rogers
Guy: There's quite an important element, a place called the KwaNobuhle pump station, which is being refurbished. Once that is complete and that's due to be completed end of this month, then we can transfer water right across the metro.
Masa: So it could happen just in time.
Guy: It could happen just in time. So we've just got to push out the days. Push out the days by really cutting our consumption.
V/O
But that is easier said than done. An 11-th hour water awareness drive from the Municipality has not been very effective… Surprisingly they’re expecting residents to drastically cut consumption when the Metro seems to be flippant in its own approach to conserving water…
Guy Rogers
We haven't been fixing leaks. There hasn't been a response to communities when they report leaks that run on for months and months and months at a time.
Masa: When we're facing a water crisis….
Guy: Absolutely… Masa: And Guy let's just take a pause on that one about the leaks. How big of a contribution is this?
Guy: Yeah. So my understanding is that nearly 30% of our water, the water we get, is being lost to leaks.
V/O
This means that … of the 280Mega L of water that Nelson Mandela Bay uses per day… a staggering 80Mega L of water is lost every single day.
Guy Rogers
There's a lot of anger that we are in this situation. But having said that, we now have a situation, of course, where the minister has come onboard where the authority is talking to private sector and they seem to be doing the right thing. Of course, time's running out even as we speak. I mean, time's running out.


V/O
Neither the Department of Water Affairs and Sanitation, nor the Nelson Mandela Bay Municipality responded to our repeated requests for interviews.

While the future of the Bay’s water remains uncertain, for many the challenges of living without running water is an ongoing daily struggle…




LINK
Not a single drop of water must go to waste… it’s a workout, I can tell you that!
V/O
The big question is… Will the lessons learnt here today be remembered when the next drought strikes…


***








PROMO 1 11”
Nelson Mandela Bay’s taps are running dry and while the region’s dams are practically empty… one cannot simply blame this crisis on the drought.

UPSOUND: I think it’s very much a mismanagement situation…
PROMO 2 21”
UPSOUND: 5 Months without running water
Nelson Mandela Bay is in crisis as taps across the Metro run dry.
UPSOUND: We have not ever been anywhere near the situation that we are at now.
But can this disaster simply be blamed on drought…
UPSOUND: It’s difficult… no rain. We must pray for rain…



PROMO 3 21”
Over 200 million liters of water are transferred over 400 kilometres on a daily basis from the Gariep dam to the drought stricken Nelson Mandela Bay Metro… a fruitless exercise if the water is not managed properly once it gets to the Bay.

UPSOUND: Nearly 30% of our water, the water we get, is being lost to leaks.

But having said that, we now have a situation, of course, where the minister has come onboard where the authority is talking to private sector and they seem to be doing the right thing. Of course, time's running out even as we speak. I mean, time's running out. V/O Neither the Department of Water Affairs and Sanitation, nor the Nelson Mandela Bay Municipality responded to our repeated requests for interviews. While the future of the Bay’s water remains uncertain, for many the challenges of living without running water is an ongoing daily struggle… LINK Not a single drop of water must go to waste… it’s a workout, I can tell you that! V/O The big question is… Will the lessons learnt here today be remembered when the next drought strikes… *** PROMO 1 11” Nelson Mandela Bay’s taps are running dry and while the region’s dams are practically empty… one cannot simply blame this crisis on the drought. UPSOUND: I think it’s very much a mismanagement situation… PROMO 2 21” UPSOUND: 5 Months without running water Nelson Mandela Bay is in crisis as taps across the Metro run dry. UPSOUND: We have not ever been anywhere near the situation that we are at now. But can this disaster simply be blamed on drought… UPSOUND: It’s difficult… no rain. We must pray for rain… PROMO 3 21” Over 200 million liters of water are transferred over 400 kilometres on a daily basis from the Gariep dam to the drought stricken Nelson Mandela Bay Metro… a fruitless exercise if the water is not managed properly once it gets to the Bay. UPSOUND: Nearly 30% of our water, the water we get, is being lost to leaks.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Nelson Mandela Bay is the said to run out of water within the next 2-3 weeks!
metadata.Unique Selling Point: It is projected that Nelson Mandela Bay (PE) will face Day Zero before the end of June! Almost 1.5 million residents will find themselves with dry taps within a matter of weeks. The dams supplying the urban areas only have about 12.3% of usable water left. Yes, we have been here before — an in the case of CT — but at least Cape Town was prepared. It seems that the bulk of Gqeberha residents are either blissfully unaware or have a head-in-the-sand approach to this looming crisis. NMBM Residents are currently using around 299ML of water per day, while demand should have been limited to around 230ML, according to experts. And the seasonal rain forecast until September doesn’t offer much hope.
metadata.Summary: Persistent drought has plagued the NMBM for over a decade. In 2010 the Metro was on the verge of a Day Zero event. Plans were made, systems suggested and residents came to the party... The threat was averted. From 2011 to 2016, the catchment areas received moderate rain and everyone forgot about the once looming crisis. But climate change has affected the region's rainfall and dam levels have been dropping. They have now reached a point of no return. With little rain forecast for the next few months, the combined usable dam levels sits at about 12% for the Metro. Taps are running dry. The city is needing to divert water earmarked for sanitation to desperate water users. Infrastructure is crumbling and continuous blackouts are not helping. It seems no lessons were learnt from 2010.
metadata.Further information: The Nelson Mandela Bay Metro replies on 4x water systems. The Kromme System supplies the main city of PE and it is estimated that the Impofu and Churchill dams have about 20 and 27 days of usable water left, respectively. The Kouga system comprises the Kouga and the Loerie dam. This system is 42% full, but not all the water is earmarked for NMB. A lot is used up by the Gamtoos Irrigation Board for farmers irrigating their crops. Then there is the much smaller Groendal dam which services Uitenhage. Recognising that NMBM would need additional water in the future, the Nooitgedacht Water Transfer Scheme was commissioned in 1993. The project that would transfer 70ML of water from the Gariep dam to the Nooitgedacht Water Treatment Works outside PE was eventually started in 2010. Destined to be completed in 2014 - at a cost of R850million - the first drops from the scheme reached the city of Gqeberha (formerly PE) in March 2022. Just in time... but this is by no means a magic bullet. The system was designed to deliver 70ML per day, and can currently deliver 190ML per day at full capacity. But there is no contingency for when the system goes down. If there is loadshedding people will simply not have water. AND.. there will not be enough for everyone.
